ent_benchmark_humanoid_foundation_model.name: Humanoid Foundation Model Benchmark
ent_benchmark_humanoid_foundation_model.summary: An independent, publicly accessible benchmark that rates and compares AI foundation models for humanoid robots across ten capability dimensions, including locomotion, manipulation, reasoning, and sim-to-real transfer.
ent_benchmark_humanoid_foundation_model.body:
## Overview

The Humanoid Foundation Model Benchmark is an independent, free, and publicly accessible benchmark platform launched by humanoid.guide on April 14, 2026, designed to rate and compare AI foundation models for humanoid robots. It employs a five-point scoring system, evaluating models across ten capability dimensions: locomotion, whole-body control, bimanual coordination, dexterous manipulation, navigation, reasoning, simulation-to-real transfer, cross-embodiment generalization, real-time inference, and long-horizon planning. It covers three model categories: VLA, world models, and reward models.

ent_benchmark_maniskill.summary: A unified benchmark for generalizable manipulation skills, providing standardized tasks, simulated environments, and evaluation protocols.
ent_benchmark_maniskill.body:
## Overview

ManiSkill is a unified evaluation benchmark for generalizable manipulation skills, providing standardized task definitions, simulation environments, and evaluation protocols. Its third-generation platform, ManiSkill3, supports large-scale evaluation through GPU-parallel physics and rendering. What it truly changes is not "how to get a manipulation task working," but "how different algorithms can be tested under reproducible, comparable, and attributable protocols"—turning manipulation skills from anecdotal demonstrations into an engineering problem amenable to quantitative comparison.

ent_benchmark_isaac_gym.body:
## Overview

The Isaac Gym benchmark is a collection of GPU-accelerated reinforcement learning benchmarks built on NVIDIA Isaac Gym, designed for high-throughput robot policy training and evaluation. What it truly changes is not the number of training algorithms, but rather liberating reinforcement learning from the CPU bottleneck of "single-environment serial sampling," enabling thousands of parallel environments to run simultaneously on a single GPU, thereby increasing training throughput by several orders of magnitude.

ent_paper_gao_a_taxonomy_for_evaluating_.name: A Taxonomy for Evaluating Generalist Robot Manipulation Policies
ent_paper_gao_a_taxonomy_for_evaluating_.name_en: A Taxonomy for Evaluating Generalist Robot Manipulation Policies
ent_paper_gao_a_taxonomy_for_evaluating_.summary: Proposes STAR-Gen, a taxonomy of visual, semantic, and behavioral generalization for visuo-lingual robot manipulation policies, and instantiates it through 1,600+ real-world trials on Bridge V2 and ALOHA 2.
ent_paper_gao_a_taxonomy_for_evaluating_.body:
## 概述

本文提出HumanoidGen框架，面向双臂+灵巧手人形机器人的全自动任务创建与演示收集，核心贡献在于将LLM规划与MCTS增强推理结合，在仿真中生成高质量、可扩展的演示数据，并构建了包含20个任务的HGen-Bench基准。作者通过空间标注、约束求解和场景缩放，解决了双臂灵巧操作中数据收集成本高、任务多样性不足的问题。

## 它改变了什么

现有机器人数据生成管线（VR遥操作、外骨骼）要求操作者具备熟练技能，且需部署大量真实物体，难以覆盖多样化任务。仿真基准如Aloha、PerAct2任务多样性有限，一般不涉及灵巧手；HumanoidBench和BiGym依赖VR或RL策略收集数据，成本高。HumanoidGen真正改变了这一局面：它不再依赖人工演示或RL探索，而是通过LLM+约束求解+MCTS的全自动管线，在仿真中生成高质量演示，将数据收集从“人工密集型”转变为“计算密集型”。

这一转变的深层意义在于：它打破了双臂灵巧操作数据收集的瓶颈，使得大规模、多样化的演示数据成为可能。作者通过空间标注（手部原子操作、资产固有信息）和约束求解，将LLM的语义理解转化为可执行的几何约束，从而在无需人工干预的情况下生成物理可行的操作序列。这为下游策略学习（如DP、DP3）提供了充足且高质量的训练数据，是迈向通用机器人操作策略的关键一步。

## 方法拆解

### 总体框架
HumanoidGen包含七个模块：空间标注、场景生成、约束生成、MCTS增强推理、数据收集、场景缩放、策略评估。

### 空间标注
- 手部原子操作标注：定义关键点和三类轴（接近轴、附着轴、平行轴）。以“捏”为例，接近轴指定手接近预捏姿态的方向，附着轴指向手指运动方向（拇指尖到食指尖），平行轴垂直于前两者且平行于手掌平面。
- 资产固有信息：指示资产自身功能（如杯子的倒水和存储功能对应不同点和…

ent_paper_kasaura_benchmarking_actor_cri.body:
## Overview
This study presents a benchmark for evaluating action-constrained reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms. In action-constrained RL, each action taken by the learning system must comply with certain constraints. These constraints are crucial for ensuring the feasibility and safety of actions in real-world systems. We evaluate existing algorithms and their novel variants across multiple robotics control environments, encompassing multiple action constraint types. Our evaluation provides the first in-depth perspective of the field, revealing surprising insights, including the effectiveness of a straightforward baseline approach. ent_paper_yang_robot_policy_evaluation_f.body:
## Overview
Current vision-based robotic simulation benchmarks have advanced manipulation research, yet general-purpose policy evaluation for real-world scenarios remains insufficient. This paper systematically reviews the challenges and requirements for designing general-purpose manipulation policy benchmarks, proposing three core solutions: adopting high visual fidelity simulation to improve transfer performance; evaluating policy robustness by progressively increasing task complexity and scene perturbations; and establishing discrete and continuous metrics to quantify the alignment between simulation and real-world performance. This framework aims to bridge the gap between simulation and real-world evaluation.

ent_paper_sunbeam_human_level_actuation_.summary: Proposes a reproducible benchmarking framework that makes 'human-level' actuation measurable for humanoids through an ISB-based DoF atlas, Human-Equivalence Envelopes (HEE), and the Human-Level Actuation Score (HLAS).
ent_paper_sunbeam_human_level_actuation_.body:
## Overview

This paper proposes the HLAS (Human-Level Actuation Score) framework, which transforms vague claims of "human-level actuation" in humanoid robots into a quantifiable, auditable, and reproducible evaluation system. Using a 75 kg, 1.75 m adult male as the reference, the framework requires robots to simultaneously meet human torque and power demands at the same joint angle and angular velocity points through the Human Equivalent Envelope (HEE). It aggregates six physical factors (ROM coverage, DoF sufficiency, HEE, bandwidth, efficiency, thermal sustainability) to output a scalar score from 0 to 1, accompanied by a four-level diagnostic structure and nine standardized measurement benchmarks.

ent_human_level_actuation_score.name: Human-Level Actuation Score
ent_human_level_actuation_score.summary: A scalar, decomposable benchmarking metric that aggregates workspace coverage, torque-power requirements, bandwidth, efficiency, and thermal sustainability to quantify how close a humanoid robot's actuation is to human-level performance.
ent_human_level_actuation_score.body:
## Overview

Human-Level Actuation Score (HLAS) is a scalar, decomposable benchmark metric that transforms vague claims about a humanoid robot's actuation capabilities being "close to human-level" into a quantifiable, auditable, and reproducible evaluation system. It uses a 75 kg, 1.75 m adult male as the reference human body, requires the robot to simultaneously satisfy human torque and power demands at the same joint angle and angular velocity points via the Human Equivalence Envelope (HEE), and aggregates six physical factors to output a scalar score from 0 to 1. What it truly changes is not "measuring who is stronger," but rather providing, for the first time, a common language for cross-laboratory and cross-platform actuation capability comparisons.

ent_kapandji_test.name: Kapandji Test
ent_kapandji_test.summary: A clinical test of thumb opposability and digital dexterity, adapted in robotics to evaluate thumb range of motion and opposition quality in dexterous robot hands.
ent_kapandji_test.body:
## Overview

The Kapandji Test is a thumb opposition assessment method originating from clinical hand surgery. It quantifies the range of motion and opposition quality of the thumb by having the subject sequentially touch specific anatomical landmarks from the index finger to the little finger with the thumb tip and scoring each touch (0–10). In robotics, this test has been adapted into a standard benchmark for dexterous hand design, used to evaluate whether a mechanical thumb can replicate the continuity and end-point precision of human opposition movements. What it truly changes is not the binary judgment of "can grasp or not," but rather the transformation of thumb function from a qualitative description into a quantitative metric comparable across platforms.

The Human-Equivalence Envelope (HEE) is a single-joint operational requirement definition method that requires a robot to simultaneously achieve human-level torque and power at the same joint angles and angular velocities within task-specific regions. ent_grasp_taxonomy.name: GRASP Taxonomy
ent_grasp_taxonomy.summary: A standardized classification system for human and robot hand grasps, used to evaluate grasp diversity and coverage in dexterous manipulation research.
ent_grasp_taxonomy.body:
## Overview

The GRASP Taxonomy is a standardized classification system for human and robotic hand grasps. It categorizes grasp actions into basic patterns—such as power grasp, precision pinch, tripod grasp, hook grasp, and lateral pinch—based on the correspondence between hand morphology and object attributes. It is used to evaluate grasp diversity and coverage in dexterous manipulation research. What it truly changes is not the physical process of "how to grasp," but the scientific language of "how to describe and compare grasps"—providing, for the first time, a commensurable unit of measurement for grasp capabilities across different laboratories, hand types, and algorithms.

ent_isb_conventions.name: ISB Conventions for Joint Coordinate Systems
ent_isb_conventions.name_en: ISB Conventions for Joint Coordinate Systems
ent_isb_conventions.summary: Standardized conventions from the International Society of Biomechanics for defining joint coordinate systems, sign conventions, and functional ranges of motion in human biomechanics.
ent_isb_conventions.body:
## Overview

The ISB Conventions for Joint Coordinate Systems are a standardized specification developed by the International Society of Biomechanics (ISB) to unify the definition of coordinate systems for human joints, rotation axis directions, sign conventions, and the measurement of functional range of motion (ROM). What it truly changes is not the measurement tools themselves, but rather transforming "human motion data" from a private format where each laboratory speaks its own language into a globally interoperable, reproducible common language—this is precisely the prerequisite for "same-reference-frame comparison" when humanoid robots use the human body as a benchmark for actuation evaluation.

ent_rom_test.name: Range of Motion Test
ent_rom_test.summary: A benchmark that measures the reachable joint angles of a robot hand or limb, used to evaluate workspace coverage and joint flexibility.
ent_rom_test.body:
## Overview

The Range of Motion Test (ROM Test) is a benchmark method for measuring the achievable angular range of each joint in a robotic hand or limb, used to quantify workspace coverage area and joint flexibility. What it truly changes is not the judgment of "whether it can move," but rather transforming "how widely it moves" from a qualitative description into a reproducible, comparable quantitative metric, providing data support for degree-of-freedom allocation, actuator selection, and morphology optimization in robotic hand design.
